title: Simple Logical Puzzles
learningGoals: Determine ordering (tallest to shortest, heaviest to lightest) from a set of comparison clues
Solve age puzzles by converting relative age statements into arithmetic
Apply if-then reasoning correctly and recognise the logical fallacy of affirming the consequent
Track direction changes after a series of left and right turns
Identify the odd-one-out based on a logical property that all others share
Chain multiple clues together to build a complete ordered sequence
coreIdeas: Comparison clues: always chain them (A > B, B > C gives A > B > C) to build a complete order
Age puzzles: assign a variable to the unknown age, then use the given relationships as equations
If-then: P implies Q does NOT mean Q implies P — the reverse is not automatically true
Directions: North → right turn → East → right turn → South → right turn → West → right turn → North
Odd-one-out: identify the single property shared by all others that the odd one lacks
Logical fallacy: All cats are animals does not mean All animals are cats

workedExamples.problem: A is taller than B. B is taller than C. Who is the shortest?
workedExamples.solution: Chain the clues: A > B > C. The smallest in the chain is C. Answer: C is the shortest.

workedExamples.problem: Riya is 3 years older than Amit. Amit is 2 years younger than Priya who is 15. How old is Riya?
workedExamples.solution: Amit = Priya − 2 = 15 − 2 = 13. Riya = Amit + 3 = 13 + 3 = 16. Answer: Riya is 16.

workedExamples.problem: You face North. Turn right. Turn right again. Which direction are you facing?
workedExamples.solution: North → turn right → East → turn right → South. Answer: South.
workedExamples.concept: Direction tracking with two right turns

workedExamples.problem: All cats are animals. Some animals are dogs. Is every cat a dog?
workedExamples.solution: No. Some animals are dogs, not all. Cats are animals but are not necessarily dogs. Answer: No.

workedExamples.problem: Dog, Cat, Lion, Table, Elephant. Find the odd one out.
workedExamples.solution: Dog, Cat, Lion, Elephant are all animals. Table is NOT an animal. Answer: Table.

onboarding.hook: Logic is a superpower — it lets you answer questions without any numbers, just pure reasoning!
onboarding.avatarIntro: Hello! I am Spark. Today we solve puzzles using pure logic — no formulas needed, just careful thinking. We will compare heights, track directions, crack age puzzles, and spot the odd one out. Let us think our way through!
onboarding.priorKnowledge: You already know how to compare numbers using greater than and less than. Today we apply that same idea to heights, ages, and weights — and extend it to directions and logical statements.

duolingoLessonArc.mission: Complete 9 exercise groups covering all six puzzle types and earn the Logic Legend badge.
duolingoLessonArc.microLessonPattern: Pose the puzzle → Draw the logic on board → Build the chain step by step → Student solves → Instant Feedback
duolingoLessonArc.rewardLoop: 10 XP per correct answer; drawing the logic diagram before answering earns 5 bonus XP.
duolingoLessonArc.reviewLoop: After group E, a flash review presents one comparison puzzle from groups A or B to reinforce the chaining technique.

uiDirectives.boardStyle: number line for comparison chains; compass rose for direction puzzles; branching diagram for if-then logic
uiDirectives.inputType: short text or multiple choice (4 options)

sessionFlow.coachHook: Three clues, three people — chain them together to find who is shortest!

boardDemo.title: A is taller than B. B is taller than C. Who is shortest?
steps: Write clue 1: A is taller than B → A > B
Write clue 2: B is taller than C → B > C
Chain: A > B > C
The rightmost (smallest) in the chain: C
Answer: C is the shortest
boardDemo.teacherLine: Always write the chain on paper: A > B > C. The person at the far right of the inequality chain is the shortest.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: A is taller than B. B is taller than C. Chain: A > B > C. Shortest is C.
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: P is shorter than Q. Q is shorter than R. Who is the tallest?  (a) P  (b) Q  (c) R  (d) Cannot determine
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct! P < Q < R. R is the tallest. Chaining clues makes it instantly clear!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Chain the clues: P < Q < R. The rightmost is the largest — R is tallest.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: If D is taller than A, extend the chain. Who is the shortest now?

sessionFlow.coachHook: Five people, four clues — build the full chain!

boardDemo.title: Raj > Priya > Amit. Sana > Priya. Sam < Amit. Order from tallest?
steps: Start with anchor chain: Raj > Priya > Amit
Add Sana: Sana > Priya, but Sana vs Raj is unknown
Add Sam: Sam < Amit → Sam is shortest
Certain: Sam is at the bottom; Priya > Amit > Sam; Raj > Priya; Sana > Priya
boardDemo.teacherLine: When relative position of two people is not given, note it as uncertain. Only state the certain facts.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Certain: Sam is shortest. Priya > Amit > Sam. Raj and Sana are both above Priya but their mutual order is unknown.
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: From the above clues, who is definitely shorter than Priya?  (a) Raj  (b) Sana  (c) Amit  (d) Sam
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct! Priya > Amit is stated directly. Amit is definitely shorter than Priya.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Raj > Priya and Sana > Priya — both are above Priya. Amit is directly below Priya in the chain: Priya > Amit.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: List all the facts you are certain about from these clues — no assumptions.

sessionFlow.coachHook: Age puzzles use subtraction and addition. Set up the number line in your head!

boardDemo.title: Riya is 3 years older than Amit. Amit is 2 years younger than Priya (age 15). How old is Riya?
steps: Given: Priya = 15
Amit = Priya − 2 = 15 − 2 = 13
Riya = Amit + 3 = 13 + 3 = 16
Riya is 16 years old
boardDemo.teacherLine: Work from the known anchor (Priya = 15) outward. First find Amit, then use Amit to find Riya.

sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Rahul is 4 years older than Meera. Meera is 3 years younger than Sana, who is 18. How old is Rahul?  (a) 19  (b) 18  (c) 17  (d) 20
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct! Sana=18, Meera=18−3=15, Rahul=15+4=19. Age chain solved!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Step 1: Meera = Sana − 3 = 18 − 3 = 15. Step 2: Rahul = Meera + 4 = 15 + 4 = 19.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: How old is Sana compared to Rahul? Write a comparison statement.

sessionFlow.coachHook: If P then Q does NOT mean if Q then P. Let us see why with a cat example!

boardDemo.title: All cats are animals. Some animals are dogs. Is every cat a dog?
steps: Draw: Cats circle inside Animals circle
Draw: Dogs circle partly overlapping Animals circle
Cats → Animals (all cats are animals, confirmed)
Some animals are dogs — but cats are in a different part of the animals circle
There is no arrow from Cats to Dogs
Answer: No, not every cat is a dog
boardDemo.teacherLine: Visualise it as circles inside circles. Cats are a subset of Animals. Dogs are also a subset of Animals. Two subsets of the same bigger group are NOT the same as each other.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Cats are inside Animals. Dogs are inside Animals. But Cats and Dogs are different subsets. Answer: No.
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: All roses are flowers. Some flowers are red. Are all roses red?  (a) Yes  (b) No  (c) Cannot determine  (d) Sometimes
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct! Roses are flowers but not all flowers are red, so we cannot conclude all roses are red.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Roses are inside Flowers. Some Flowers are Red. This does not guarantee Roses are Red.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Make up your own if-then statement and show why the reverse is not necessarily true.

sessionFlow.coachHook: Same technique as height — build the chain from all the clues!

boardDemo.title: P > Q, Q > R, R > S, S > T. Who is 3rd heaviest?
steps: Chain: P > Q > R > S > T
Order from heaviest: P (1st), Q (2nd), R (3rd), S (4th), T (5th)
3rd heaviest = R
boardDemo.teacherLine: When clues are given in a clean chain, simply write the chain and count positions.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Chain: P > Q > R > S > T. 3rd from the top = R.
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: A > B > C > D > E. Who is 4th lightest (2nd heaviest)?  (a) A  (b) B  (c) D  (d) E
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct! Order: A (1st heaviest), B (2nd heaviest = 4th lightest). Answer is B.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: With 5 people, 4th lightest = 2nd heaviest. Heaviest is A, 2nd heaviest is B.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: In the chain P > Q > R > S > T, what is R's rank from the lightest end?

sessionFlow.coachHook: Every right turn rotates you 90 degrees clockwise. Track it step by step!

boardDemo.title: Face North. Turn right. Turn right again. Which direction?
steps: Start: facing North
Turn right (90 degrees clockwise): now facing East
Turn right again (90 degrees clockwise): now facing South
Answer: South
boardDemo.teacherLine: Draw a compass: N at top, E at right, S at bottom, W at left. Each right turn moves you one step clockwise around the compass.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: North → right → East → right → South. Final direction: South.
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: You face East. Turn left. Turn left again. Which direction are you facing?  (a) North  (b) South  (c) West  (d) East
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct! East → left → North → left → West. Two left turns from East = West.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Each left turn moves 90 degrees anti-clockwise. East → left = North. North → left = West.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Starting from South, how many right turns does it take to face East?

visual.caption: Group F for Simple Logical Puzzles.

sessionFlow.coachHook: Four things share a property. One does not. Find the outsider!

boardDemo.title: Dog, Cat, Lion, Table, Elephant — find the odd one out.
steps: Check Dog: is it an animal? Yes
Check Cat: animal? Yes
Check Lion: animal? Yes
Check Table: animal? No — it is furniture
Check Elephant: animal? Yes
Odd one out: Table
boardDemo.teacherLine: State the shared property of the group first. Here: all are animals. Then find the one that does NOT have that property.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Dog, Cat, Lion, Elephant are all animals. Table is not an animal. Odd one out = Table.
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Cricket, Football, Chess, Basketball, Hockey — find the odd one out.  (a) Cricket  (b) Chess  (c) Football  (d) Hockey
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct! Cricket, Football, Basketball, Hockey are all physical outdoor sports. Chess is a non-physical indoor board game. Chess is the odd one out.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: All others are physical outdoor sports. Chess is a board game — not physical, not outdoor.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Make your own odd-one-out puzzle with 5 items and challenge a friend.

visual.caption: Group G for Simple Logical Puzzles.

sessionFlow.coachHook: Watch out — knowing the result does not always tell you the cause!

boardDemo.title: If it rains, the ground is wet. The ground is wet. Did it rain?
steps: Given: Rain → Ground wet
Observed: Ground is wet
Question: Does that mean it rained?
No! Ground could be wet from a pipe leak, sprinkler, or flood
This is the logical fallacy called Affirming the Consequent
Answer: Not necessarily
boardDemo.teacherLine: P → Q (rain causes wet ground). Seeing Q (wet ground) does NOT prove P (rain). Other causes could produce the same result.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Rain → Ground wet. But Ground wet does not reverse to: definitely rained. Other causes exist. Answer: Not necessarily.
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: If a student studies hard, they pass the exam. Raj passed the exam. Did Raj study hard?  (a) Yes, definitely  (b) No, impossible  (c) Not necessarily  (d) Yes, always
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct! Raj may have passed due to luck or prior knowledge. The statement only guarantees that studying leads to passing, not the reverse.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Study → Pass does NOT mean Pass → Studied. Raj passed, but we cannot conclude he studied hard. This is the affirming-the-consequent fallacy.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Give a real-life example of affirming the consequent — a false reverse conclusion.

sessionFlow.coachHook: Five quick deduction questions — identify the type and solve fast!

boardDemo.title: Speed Logic Strategy
steps: Comparison puzzle: write the chain immediately
Direction puzzle: draw a mini compass
Age puzzle: start from the known age
If-then: never reverse without checking
Odd-one-out: state the shared property first
boardDemo.teacherLine: Identifying the puzzle type takes 3 seconds but prevents wasted effort on the wrong approach.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Read, identify type, apply the right technique, answer.
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: M is heavier than N. N is heavier than O. O is heavier than P. Who is the 2nd lightest?  (a) M  (b) N  (c) O  (d) P
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Perfect! Chain: M > N > O > P. From lightest: P (1st), O (2nd). Speed round champion!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Chain: M > N > O > P. From lightest: P is 1st lightest, O is 2nd lightest. Answer: O.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Explain in two sentences how you would approach a 5-clue ordering problem in an exam.

beats.teacherLine: Here is a puzzle: All birds can fly. Penguins are birds. Can penguins fly? Most people say yes — but the answer is NO! Penguins are birds but cannot fly. This is why we cannot blindly apply logic rules without thinking carefully. Today we learn to think carefully and catch those traps!
boardSteps: Write: All birds can fly. Penguins are birds.
Reveal: No! The first statement is actually false.
Lesson: Always question the premises, not just the logic
